When an agent chooses the wrong moment.

Holding a stock often and holding it at favorable moments are different behaviors. RetailAgent separates exposure from timing to audit sequential LLM decisions.

RetailAgent: Structured Adverse Timing in Self-Conditioned Multimodal LLM Trading Agents

Yupeng Zhang, Liuyuan Jiang, Hongyi Huang, Bingheng Li, Lisha Chen

PaperVideo storyboard

The takeaway

RetailAgent audits sequential long-or-flat decisions using within-stock timing after removing average exposure. The paper reports negative timing and studies how it changes with trajectory shuffling and self-authored memory.

01Explanation

Audit a trading agent’s timing, not just its exposure

Exposure and timing answer different questions

Suppose an agent is long during half of the intervals in a trading day. Its return depends on what the stock did and on which half it chose. Comparing it with a policy that holds the stock at half exposure throughout the same day separates a timing component from the average amount invested.

Decide first, observe the next return afterward

RetailAgent gives the LLM an anonymized intraday history and condition-specific state. The agent then chooses long or flat before the next interval return is revealed. Concealing stock identity and other information keeps the decision boundary controlled and makes the tested policy easier to interpret.

01

Control the information

Show anonymized intraday history, then require a long-or-flat decision before the next return.

02

Remove mean exposure

Compare each schedule with constant exposure on the same realized stock-day.

03

Disrupt the sequence

Shuffle saved actions and examine matched memory panels to characterize sequential structure.

Subtract average exposure

The timing score sums each following return multiplied by the action minus that stock-day’s mean action. A negative score means exposure was allocated to relatively unfavorable intervals on that path. The score is a diagnostic of alignment, rather than a complete accounting of an executable strategy’s profitability.

Shuffle the schedule to test the alignment

Same-day shuffling preserves a stock-day’s action count while disrupting interval alignment. Global shuffling provides a different control. In the principal text condition, both controls attenuate the negative timing. The study also examines memory and persistence using matched panels; those comparisons need their stated conditioning and sampling frames.

Keep the conclusion at the level tested

The paper documents negative timing across tested configurations and recoverable structure in action traces. It does not resolve how another participant would exploit that structure in a live market with costs and feedback. The contribution is a controlled behavioral audit and a way to study the timing of sequential decisions.

The comparison stays on the same price path

A stock’s overall movement affects both an agent and a constant-exposure comparator. Subtracting that comparator focuses the score on when the agent allocated its exposure. Negative timing means relatively unfavorable allocation on the evaluated path.

02Interactive

Explore the idea

Same exposure, different timing

Toggle whether a toy agent is long or flat before each interval. Returns are fixed at −20, +15, −10, +25, −15, and +5 basis points.

Computed using the paper’s timing formula on six synthetic returns. This is not a trading simulation or empirical RetailAgent result. Inverting a schedule negates its centered timing score.

03Results

Negative timing attenuates under shuffling

Table 1, principal 10-minute Qwen3.5 text condition. The intact condition contains 13,710 stock-days. The reported 95% interval for intact timing is [−49.4, −41.8] bps. The chart compares the magnitudes of negative timing, with the signed values printed explicitly.

The matched memory analyses also examine persistence and timing conditional on switching. They help describe the behavior of the tested agents; they do not turn this audit into a live-market profitability result.

Table 1 · Text timing and shuffle controls in the paper

How to read this result

These scores are research timing measures on the evaluated historical paths. The paper leaves transaction costs, market impact, strategic feedback, and whether the pattern remains actionable to further study. Magnitudes from different sampling frames are descriptive comparisons.

04A closer look

Inside the method

A(p, r) = Σₜ (pₜ − p̄) rₜ, where p̄ = (1/T) Σₜ pₜ.

pₜ is 1 for long and 0 for flat, and rₜ is the following interval return. The score compares a binary schedule with constant exposure p̄ on the same realized path. Basis points are used for the interactive toy returns.

pₜ
A binary decision: long (1) or flat (0).
p̄
Average exposure on that stock-day.
rₜ
The interval return observed after the action.
A(p, r)
Timing relative to constant exposure p̄ on that path.

The technical idea

Center the action sequence

For a stock-day, p̄ is the fraction of intervals spent long. The constant-exposure comparator earns p̄ times the sum of interval returns. Subtracting it from the schedule’s return gives the timing sum shown below.

Separate direction from sequential alignment

A policy that is always long or always flat has zero centered timing. A nonzero score requires variation in its actions and alignment with subsequent returns. This explains why action persistence and switching behavior matter to the audit.

Read controls within their sampling frame

Same-day shuffling preserves each day’s action count while breaking interval alignment. Global shuffling is a different control. The paper’s modalities and memory panels do not all use identical stock-day frames, so their magnitudes need the stated conditioning and sample counts.

Assumptions and guarantee

This is an empirical audit of directional and sequential policy structure under a controlled information boundary. Its timing measure is defined in Equation 1. It does not establish a theorem about all LLM trading policies.

Equation 1 · Timing decomposition in the paper

How this connects to the other papers

RetailAgent focuses on the timing of sequential choices. SURF offers another view of decision quality: how well a set of choices represents different objective trade-offs.
